questions.q: Two requests each read Ada's balance (₦50,000) into JavaScript, subtract their amount, and write the result back with update … set balance = $1. What is this bug called?
questions.explain: Read-modify-write in the application is the classic lost update. Each statement is correct; the gap between the read and the write is not protected.
options: A lost update: the second write is based on a stale read and erases the first

questions.q: Which statement debits safely even when many sessions run it on the same row at once, in the default isolation level?
questions.explain: The new value is computed from the current row, and the check is part of the where. A second session waits for the row lock and re-checks the condition against the committed new balance. The unconditional version checks nothing: it overdraws the account unless a check constraint refuses it with an error instead of a clean "not enough money".
options: update accounts set balance_kobo = $1 where id = $2 with a balance computed in JavaScript
update accounts set balance_kobo = balance_kobo - $1 where id = $2 and balance_kobo >= $1
select balance_kobo from accounts where id = $2 followed by an if and an update
update accounts set balance_kobo = balance_kobo - $1 where id = $2 without a condition, relying on nothing else

questions.q: A transfer debits Ada, then the credit to Tunde fails. Which ACID property makes sure Ada's debit is undone?
questions.explain: Atomicity means all or nothing: when any statement in the transaction fails and it rolls back, every change in it is undone.

questions.q: What does durability mean in PostgreSQL?
questions.explain: PostgreSQL confirms a commit only after its WAL records are safely on disk. After a crash, replaying the WAL restores every committed change.
options: Once commit returns, the change survives a crash, because it was written to the write-ahead log and flushed to disk first
Every row keeps all its old versions forever

questions.q: You wrap the naive read-then-write transfer in begin … commit on a real server, at the default isolation level. Is the lost update fixed?
questions.explain: The lesson's lost-update.js shows it: ₦30,000 appeared in read committed although both sessions used transactions. You need relative conditional writes, row locks, a version check, or a stricter level with retries.
options: Yes: transactions are isolated, so two of them cannot interfere
No: in read committed both transactions can still read ₦50,000 before either writes, and the second write overwrites the first
Yes, but only on PostgreSQL 17 or later

questions.q: Can a PostgreSQL transaction see another transaction's uncommitted changes (a dirty read)?
questions.explain: MVCC gives every statement a snapshot of committed data only. PostgreSQL has no mode that exposes uncommitted rows.
options: No: PostgreSQL accepts read uncommitted but behaves as read committed

questions.q: In read committed, a transaction reads Ada's balance, another session commits a debit, and the transaction reads again. What does the second read return?
questions.explain: That is a non-repeatable read. Repeatable read would keep the first snapshot for the whole transaction and return the same value twice.
options: The same value as the first read
The new, committed value: each statement takes a fresh snapshot
An error, because the row changed

questions.q: A report counts transfers over ₦10,000, then sums them, in two statements. Meanwhile another session inserts a large transfer. The count and the sum disagree. Which anomaly is this, and which level prevents it?
questions.explain: A phantom is a new row appearing in a repeated query with the same condition. Repeatable read gives the whole transaction one snapshot, so both statements describe the same moment.

questions.q: Two transactions each check that the family total is at least ₦40,000, then each withdraws ₦40,000 from a different wallet. Both commit in repeatable read, and the total goes negative. Why did repeatable read not stop it?
questions.explain: Repeatable read detects two transactions updating the same row. Write skew needs serializable, which tracks read/write dependencies, or explicit locks on every row the decision depends on.
options: Repeatable read does not use snapshots
They wrote different rows, so there was no write conflict to detect; each decided on data the other then changed (write skew)

questions.q: A repeatable read or serializable transaction fails with SQLSTATE 40001. What should the application do?
questions.explain: A serialization failure means "you lost a race, nothing you did was kept". Retrying the whole transaction makes it read fresh data and decide again.
options: Report a bug: the SQL is wrong
Retry only the statement that failed
Roll back and run the whole transaction again, from its first read, usually after a short backoff
Switch the connection to read committed and continue

questions.q: Session A runs select … from accounts where id = 1 for update and keeps its transaction open. What happens when session B runs a plain select balance_kobo from accounts where id = 1?
questions.explain: Row locks block other writers and other lockers (for update, update, delete), never plain readers. That is the benefit of MVCC.
options: B returns immediately with the last committed balance
B fails with a lock error

questions.q: When do you need select … for update instead of a single conditional update?
questions.explain: Locking first turns a multi-step check into a safe one: every read after the lock sees current data, and nobody else can change those rows in between.
options: Never: conditional updates are always enough
When the decision needs several reads or steps (limits, fees, audit rows) and must be based on data nobody can change until you commit
When you want other sessions to see your changes early

questions.q: Several workers poll a payout_jobs table. Which query lets each worker take a different job without waiting for the others?
questions.explain: Without a lock, two workers take the same job. With a plain for update, they queue behind each other on the first job. nowait makes them fail. skip locked moves past rows another worker holds.
options: select id from payout_jobs where status = 'queued' limit 1
select id from payout_jobs where status = 'queued' limit 1 for update
select id from payout_jobs where status = 'queued' order by id limit 1 for update skip locked
select id from payout_jobs where status = 'queued' limit 1 for update nowait

questions.q: Transfer A (Ada → Tunde) and transfer B (Tunde → Ada) run at the same time and one fails with 40P01. What caused it?
questions.explain: A deadlock is a cycle in the "waits for" relation. PostgreSQL detects it after deadlock_timeout and aborts one transaction so the other can finish.
options: Both transfers used the same connection
Each locked its sender's row first and then waited for the other's row, which the other transaction held: a cycle of waits
The isolation level was too strict

questions.q: What is the standard way to prevent that deadlock?
questions.explain: If every transaction takes its locks in the same global order, no cycle can form: whoever gets the first lock goes ahead, the other waits while holding nothing. Retrying on 40P01 is still wise for the cases you did not foresee.
options: Lock both accounts at the start, always in the same order, for example by ascending id

questions.q: A support agent opens a customer's settings form, edits for five minutes, and saves. How should you stop them overwriting a change made in the meantime?
questions.explain: No database lock or transaction can span five minutes of user think time. A version check detects the conflict at save time, and the application can show the newer data.
options: Hold a for update lock while the form is open
Use serializable isolation for the save
Optimistic concurrency: send the row's version with the form and update only where version = $expected, increasing it
Nothing: the last save should always win
Save every field in its own transaction

questions.q: Over HTTP, how is a version conflict usually expressed?
questions.explain: ETags are the HTTP form of the version column. 412 (or 409) tells the client to reload and try again with fresh data.
options: The client sends If-Match with the version (ETag) it read; the server answers 412 Precondition Failed if it no longer matches
The server silently applies the newer change
The client sends If-None-Match: * on every request

questions.q: A retry helper catches 40001. Which code should run again on each attempt?
questions.explain: The failed attempt decided on data that has since changed. Only rerunning the reads lets the next attempt decide correctly. It also means the function must not have outside side effects, such as sending an SMS.
options: The whole transaction function: begin, all reads, the decision, the writes and commit

questions.q: A mobile app's transfer request times out, and the app sends it again. Can the server simply run the transfer a second time?
questions.explain: A database retry after 40001 is safe because nothing was committed. A client retry after a timeout is different: the outcome is unknown. Idempotency keys (API engineering course) solve that.
options: No: the first attempt may have committed; the request needs an idempotency key so the server can recognise the repeat
Yes, if the isolation level is serializable
No, the server must always refuse a second request

questions.q: Why should you never call a payment provider's HTTP API inside a database transaction?
questions.explain: External calls can take seconds or hang. Meanwhile row locks block other transfers and the connection is unavailable. Record intent in the database, commit, call the provider, then record the result in a second transaction.
options: HTTP calls are not allowed by PostgreSQL
The transaction holds its locks and its pooled connection for the whole call, making others wait; and a rollback cannot undo the external call
The provider would see uncommitted data

questions.q: In pg_stat_activity you find a session that has been idle in transaction for 40 minutes. Why is that a problem?
questions.explain: A forgotten open transaction pins old snapshots and locks. idle_in_transaction_session_timeout ends such sessions automatically.
options: It uses a lot of CPU
It may hold locks others wait for, and while it is open PostgreSQL cannot clean up old row versions, so tables bloat
It blocks all reads on the server
It is harmless; idle means doing nothing

questions.q: With the pg pool, why must begin, the queries and commit all go through one client from pool.connect()?
questions.explain: If begin runs on connection 1 and the update on connection 2, the update runs outside the transaction and commits immediately. Take one client, use it for the whole transaction, and release it in finally.
options: A transaction belongs to one connection, and separate pool.query calls may use different connections
Because a pool runs everything serially
It is only a style convention

questions.q: Two read-then-write debits interleave on one PGlite connection. What does this print?
questions.explain: Both reads ran before either write, so both saw 100,000. The second write, 100,000 − 30,000, replaced the first, so the 20,000 debit vanished: a lost update.

questions.q: The same two debits, written as relative updates. What does this print?
questions.explain: Each update computes the new value from the row as it is when the update runs, so both debits count. On a real server the second update waits for the first's row lock and then applies to the new value.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Two seats, three bookings. The condition free > 0 is checked against the current row by each update, so the third finds 0 free seats and changes nothing. affectedRows tells the application who got a seat.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The credit ran first and succeeded, then the debit broke the check constraint. The transaction rolled back as a whole, so the credit was undone too.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Catching the duplicate-key error in JavaScript does not repair the transaction. PostgreSQL refuses the next statement with 25P02, the transaction rolls back, and even the first insert is gone.

questions.q: The same code with a savepoint. What does this print?
questions.explain: Rolling back to the savepoint undoes only the failed statement and clears the error state, so the transaction continues and commits both good inserts.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The first save moved the version to 2, so the second save, still expecting version 1, changed nothing. After reloading (expecting 2) the third save succeeded and moved the version to 3.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A report transaction can declare itself read only; any write is refused with 25006. Repeatable read gives the report one consistent snapshot.

questions.q: What does this one-statement transfer print?
questions.explain: The second debit found only 10,000 left, so debit was empty. The credit's exists was false, and the insert selected from an empty join: no transfer row, no credit, and the application sees 0 rows returned.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The rolled-back transaction used ids 1 and 2 (the failed insert still drew a number before its check failed). Sequences are never rolled back, so gaps are normal. Never use ids to count transfers or to detect missing ones.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The deadlock on attempt 1 is retryable. The unique violation on attempt 2 is not: retrying would fail the same way, so the helper rethrows it at once.

questions.q: Prevent transfer deadlocks. Write lockOrder(fromId, toId) that returns the two account ids in the order they must be locked (ascending), whatever the direction of the transfer, and refuses a transfer to the same account by throwing an Error.
questions.explain: Both directions lock account 3 first, so two opposite transfers can never each hold one row and wait for the other. In SQL: select … where id = any($1) order by id for update.
questions.expected:
[ 3, 7 ] [ 3, 7 ]
cannot transfer to the same account

questions.q: PostgreSQL finds deadlocks by looking for a cycle in the "waits for" graph. Write findCycle(waitsFor), where waitsFor maps each transaction to the one it waits for (or nothing). Return the list of transactions in the first cycle found, starting from the lowest key, or null.
questions.explain: Follow the waits from each transaction; coming back to the start means a cycle. Transaction 104 waits too, but it is not part of the cycle: aborting any one of 101, 102 or 103 unblocks everybody, which is what the deadlock detector does.

questions.q: Implement optimistic concurrency on an in-memory store. save(store, id, changes, expectedVersion) applies the changes and increases the version only if the stored version equals expectedVersion; it returns "saved v<new version>" or "conflict".
questions.explain: The compare-and-set must be one step. In SQL that is update … set …, version = version + 1 where id = $1 and version = $2, checked with the number of affected rows.
questions.expected:
saved v2
conflict
saved v3
{ id: 1, dailyLimitKobo: 20000000, version: 3 }

questions.q: Write the reconciliation check. reconcile(opening, balances, transfers) returns the ids of accounts whose current balance is not opening + incoming − outgoing, and also whether the total of all balances is unchanged.
questions.explain: Account 3 should hold ₦25,000 but holds ₦30,000, and the total grew by ₦5,000: some code path credited it without a transfer row. Both checks are cheap enough to run every night on the real ledger.

questions.q: Model MVCC. Each row version has the transaction number that committed it. Write visible(versions, snapshot) that returns the value of the newest version committed at or before snapshot, or undefined if none. Then show a repeatable-read transaction (snapshot 10) and a read-committed statement run later (snapshot 12) reading the same row.
questions.explain: Old versions stay until no snapshot can need them. A repeatable-read transaction keeps its snapshot, so it keeps seeing ₦50,000; read committed takes a new snapshot per statement and sees the debit. It is also why a long-open transaction stops old versions from being cleaned up.
questions.expected:
repeatable read (snapshot 10): 5000000
read committed, next statement (snapshot 12): 2000000
before the account existed (snapshot 2): undefined

questions.q: Replay an interleaving. Each step is ["read", tx] (the transaction reads the balance into its own variable) or ["write", tx, amount] (it writes "its read value minus amount"). Write replay(start, steps) that returns the final balance, and compare a safe schedule with an overlapping one.
questions.explain: Same operations, different order, different result: that is what makes a schedule unsafe. In the overlapping one, B's write is based on a read taken before A wrote, so A's debit of 30,000 is lost. Serializable isolation only lets a set of transactions commit if the result matches some serial order.

questions.q: Simulate for update skip locked. Write claim(jobs, locked) that returns the id of the first queued job (lowest id) that is not in the locked set, or null, and use it to let two workers claim jobs in turns until none are left.
questions.explain: Each worker skips jobs another worker holds instead of waiting on them, so no job is taken twice and nobody blocks. In PostgreSQL the "locked set" is the row locks held by other open transactions.
